messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Parole Officer
  trauma_type: Police violence
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Moral Violation: People misbehaving, Stress: Stress, Somatic (Heart Racing): Own heart racing or pounding
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Scanning for Danger: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
  Memory: Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
  Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Institutional Failure: The people or institutions that should have protected me let me down

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At 54, Daniel had spent most of his adult life trying to live by order, procedure, and restraint, which made what happened to him on a winter night still feel, in his telling, like a violation not only of his body but of everything he believed the job stood for. He was working as a parole officer in a cramped county office on the edge of town when he was taken aside during a routine transport by officers he knew from years of coordination with local law enforcement. A disagreement about a client’s behavior escalated in front of him, and he watched police use force that, in his view, went far beyond any need for control. He remembered the flash of a hallway light, the echo of raised voices, then the hard impact of being shoved and pinned while someone he had trusted as a professional ally acted with a cruelty that left him stunned. From that night on, Daniel came to believe he had been betrayed by someone he trusted, that what happened to him was deeply unfair and nothing had been done about it, and that the very people and institutions meant to protect him had let him down. Those beliefs settled quickly into his account of the event; he could not think about it without moving back and forth between anger and a kind of stunned disbelief, as though the details themselves were intolerable and proof of a larger injustice.

In the weeks that followed, ordinary moments at work began to carry a charge they had not had before. If a supervisee arrived late, spoke back, or acted disrespectfully, Daniel felt a flash of heat and a tightening in his chest, as if misbehavior itself announced that something dangerous was underway. He had come to read stress in the office as a warning sign, and when his own heart started racing during a tense meeting or after a difficult phone call, it confirmed for him that he was not simply uneasy but that danger might be near. That bodily alarm made him think again of betrayal and unfairness, and it sharpened his sense that he had been left unprotected; at the same time, it made any unruly behavior feel bigger, less containable, and more personally threatening than it might have once seemed. He began to scan his surroundings constantly for signs of danger, watching doorways, hands, tone of voice, and the mood in a room before he could fully register what was happening. Unusual silence was especially hard for him. If a hallway at the office went quiet or a room fell still, he felt something dangerous was about to happen, and that silence could pull him back toward the memory he tried not to fully recall. He found himself pushing the memory away before he could complete it, because once it came close, it felt so extreme that it was hard to believe it had actually happened to him; the event existed in his mind as an incomplete picture, with certain fragments vivid and the rest missing, as though the mind had broken away from it to protect itself. Yet the fragments he could not fully hold onto—boots on tile, the force of being controlled, the sense of humiliation—were enough to keep the injustice alive, and the more he tried to suppress the memory, the more his body and thoughts seemed to circle back to the same conclusion that he had been wronged and abandoned.

Over months, Daniel’s life narrowed around that loop. On his commute he avoided traffic jams and anything that made him feel trapped; at work he kept conversations brief, stood near exits, and preferred to review files alone rather than stay in rooms where silence might suddenly fall. His wife noticed that he became jumpy at home, too, startling when a refrigerator door slammed or when the house went quiet at night. Even when he tried to rest, his attention drifted outward, scanning, waiting, and the work of staying alert made him feel as if the danger had never really ended. What troubled him most was that the same bodily surge, the same racing heart, could send him back into the story of being betrayed, unfairly treated, and failed by the institutions around him. At those moments, people misbehaving at work or on the street no longer looked merely rude or difficult; they looked like evidence that the world remained hostile and that he could still be caught off guard. The memory, always partial and half-repulsed, fed the sense that something had been covered over or left unresolved, and that unresolved quality fed his outrage and his watchfulness in turn. He became more certain that he could not trust silence, authority, or his own body when it warned him.

By the time he finally sought help, Daniel was no longer able to dismiss the pattern as stress from a demanding job. He came in after a week in which a young supervisee’s defiance at the office set off his heart racing, made him scan the room for danger, and left him preoccupied with the old sense of being betrayed all day. At home he had begun to dread quiet evenings, because the silence in the house seemed to press the memory toward him again, fragments and all, and he no longer wanted his wife to see how quickly he was startled. He was hoping, cautiously, to make sense of why these moments still hit so hard and to regain some confidence that he could do his work without feeling constantly on guard. What he feared most was that the same unfairness and abandonment would keep repeating itself—that he would stay trapped between the half-remembered event and the certainty that, once again, no one would protect him.
